Manganese Hampers

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They're shareholders in the 4th largest manganese mine in South Africa, but instead of annual dividends, all they get is R1000 a year and a Christmas food hamper.

Unique Selling Point:
Interviews with some of the 540 community members who were promised education bursaries, job opportunities, health care and upliftment of their 27 villages when they became shareholders in Pitsa ya Setshaba (The Community Pot) the entity that was awarded the prospecting rights for the United Manganese of Kalahari mine near Hotazel. According to legislation, this mining community Trust (KCT) was established as a pre-requisite to prospecting and mining rights. Two busloads of villagers (+- 150 people) were taken to Pretoria to meet Dept of Mineral Resources Minister Susan Shabangu in 2005, as evidence of community involvement and benefit. Instead of enrichment they are still living in abject poverty and only a select few are benefiting from the hugely profitable mine.

Summary:
In 2004 Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg arrived in South Africa looking for manganese mining opportunities and a BEE partner who could win the mining rights. Several ANC-connected entities jostled for the privilege. Lazarus Mbethe representing Pitsa ya Setshaba won the privilege, but his consortium had to include the ANC's Chancellor House and the Kuruman Community Trust. Together they owned 51% of UMK in a company called Majestic Silver Trading. Viktor Vekselberg's Renova owned 49% and invested $350m to build the mine. In a 2006 State visit to South Africa President Vladimir Putin consolidated this partnership, with Vekselberg promising to invest a further $2billion for a manganese smelter at Coega.
UMK is now a fabulously profitable mine (R2.4 billion a year) but the community are receiving very little benefit. Individuals receive R1000 a year, and a Christmas food hamper.
Lazarus Mbethe is the sole Trustee of the Kuruman Community Trust, but the community never see any financial statements. They believe they were simply used to get the mining rights to make ANC comrades rich, while they continue to live lives of hardship - in villages with no running water, no electricity, no inside toilets, no jobs, and surviving only on pensions and government grants.
The KCT boasts only three community projects: the goat project - now defunct; the brick making project - taken over by a private individual, and the mobile clinic project - still operational but only in villages that already have a clinic. Most of the people I met with didn't know of its existence and only one person had never seen it. It is parked in the grounds of the


Further information:
The ANC benefit hugely from the UMK mine, being the recipients of annual donations by UMK, Chancellor House, and Majestic Silver Trading. It is clear from meeting minutes as far back as 2007 that the ANC regards this mine as and ANC mine, and villagers are scared to speak up saying "they can kill us".
The ANC's reluctance to condemn Russia's invasion of Ukraine is partly explained by their partnership with Renova in this mine. They are dependent on the Russians for their income.


Extra Budget Items:
Travel, care hire and accommodation to Kuruman
Extra shoot days (2 days Kuruman & possibly 2 days Johannesburg & Pretoria)
Translation of community interviews from Setswana to English

Script:


LET THEM EAT PAP – FINAL

V/O: Imagine being told you’ve been chosen as a beneficiary of a manganese mine. You and 20 other people in your village are now part of a Trust. Your lives will change, you will be lifted out of poverty, and when the mine opens, you’ll be employed. You even get bused all the way to Pretoria to meet the Deputy Minister of Mineral Resources.

Doreen: She said I don’t want to hear any child from Kuruman saying they are struggling to get a job, because we are issuing a mining license.

Pause for sound of explosion

V/O: Eighteen years later the mine is flourishing, but you are still unemployed and struggling to survive.

FADE TO BLACK

Tidimalo: You can see the house we live in. They’re not houses that should be housing seven people. This house is too small for seven people.

V/O: Poverty has settled on the Moncho family like a second skin. We met Tidimalo going to fetch water, but the only tap in the village was dry. It makes it harder to care for her sick father who is frail and confined to bed.

Sfx: Tidimalo talking to her Dad

Tidimalo: We survive on my dad’s social grant, and the kids’ social grant – only. No one in our family works. That means when my dad dies…it’s a story.

V/O: The Northern Cape has rampant unemployment, few opportunities, and a growing alcohol and drug problem. But beneath this red soil lies 80% of the world’s manganese. It’s a booming industry – so why is this community still poor?

When mining rights were nationalized in 2004, it presented huge opportunities for black empowerment. Stefaans Brümmer was a journalist for the Mail & Guardian at the time.

Stefaans: The Department of Minerals said it’s going to give these rights only to BEE companies, and then a technical and financial partner would be brought in after the award of the mining rights.

V/O: Enter billionaire Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg, owner of the Renova Group – a conglomerate with interests in telecoms, energy and – yes - mining.

Stefaans: So Vekselberg is a typical Russian oligarch.

V/O: The oligarchs are politically influential businessmen who made their fortunes when state-run industries were privatised, after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Stefaans: So, Vekselberg made his money out of oil fields and especially bauxite mining.

V/O: In 2004 Vekselberg was worth $10 billion. He splashed out on nine priceless Fabergé eggs which are housed in his private museum in St Petersburg. He also visited South Africa for the first time - on the lookout for mining investment opportunities.

Stefaans: He met amongst others the Mining Minster Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka at the time, and Thabo Mbeki, the President at the time.

Masa: So, he had access to some powerful people?

Stefaans: Clearly, he had some diplomatic backing also from the Russian side, and I think he was able to make a grand entrance.
Text: “Renova masters Africa” headline

V/O: Vekselberg’s attention was directed to the Northern Cape manganese fields by an investment arm of the ANC - Chancellor House - named after the building in downtown Joburg that originally housed the law firm of Mandela and Tambo.
00:08:24
Stefaans: Chancellor House was set up around 2003. It was set up simply to fund the ANC. And I think there were a number of meetings between Renova and ANC officials.

V/O: He also met Lazarus Mbethe, a politically connected businessman from Mpumalanga involved in coal mining, security and farming. Mbethe’s company Pitsa ya Setshaba – meaning community pot - applied for the mining rights, but these could only be awarded if the local Kuruman community was included in the venture.

Nelson: People of Kuruman were exploited.

V/O: Nelson Hantise is the Chairperson of the John Taole Gaetsewe Civic Organisation.

Nelson: Mbethe pushed to open the mine, to say you are the local people, you are the beneficiary, or you are the shareholder. Come, come, come, come, I’m opening the mine, help me to get the licence.

V/O: The Kuruman Community Trust was founded by Mbethe in 2005. He selected 20 people from 27 villages around the Kuruman area - a total of 540 beneficiaries. He bused representatives from each village to the DMR in Pretoria.

Motlalepula: When we went there, they said we are going to sign for the opening of the mine.

V/O: Motlalepula Mosetlo was one of the beneficiaries on the bus.

Motlalepula: And when the mine opened, they will take us first – we who are suffering and uneducated - to work at the mine.

V/O: With promises of employment, education, roads and clinics, Doreen Ntsheyagae felt they were on the road to the promised land.

Masa: When you left there, were you happy?

Doreen: Yes, we were very happy, like the children of Canaan coming from Egypt, promised gold and silver. But we didn’t know what was going to happen. We only knew that there is a mine, and when they talk about a mine it means work.

V/O: And so it came to pass, that United Manganese of Kalahari opened in 2005, with Lazarus Mbethe as Chairman of a joint venture between Renova and BEE partner Majestic Silver Trading 40 – a consortium with strong political links. Majestic Silver Trading is made up of Chancellor House and Pitsa ya Setshaba, with Kuruman Community Trust getting 8% of the shares.

Stefaans: Vekselberg’s relationship with the ANC, getting into bed with Chancellor House for example, I don’t think it is necessarily because he believes in what the ANC stands for. It was simply sucking up to power. That’s what oligarchs do.

V/O: The Brenthurst Foundation’s Ray Hartley agrees.

Ray: There are people within the ANC who admire the Russian oligarchic system where you have a political elite and a bunch of elite businesses around that are making a lot of money out of that elite, and contracts being shared amongst friends and all that kind of thing, which is the way Russia works.

V/O: In 2006 Russian President Vladimir Putin came to South Africa on a State Visit, accompanied by a large business delegation. Leading that delegation was none other than Viktor Vekselberg with promises of investment in infrastructure.

And money talks. The licence was granted and UMK started mining in 2008. Five years later they celebrated their joint venture.

Mbethe: I believe our mine it’s a real Northern Cape success story. Indeed, a South African success story.

Konstantin: UMK mine is the most positive example of cooperation between Russia and South Africa.

V/O: Cooperation witnessed by Presidents Putin and Zuma when Viktor Vekselberg and Lazarus Mbethe signed agreements in Durban.

Link: This is the mine that has rained riches on its Russian and South African shareholders – as much as R2.4 billion a year. But while they’ve been divvying up the dosh, it seems the local community that was used to unlock that wealth has been left out in the cold.

Dineo: The people were used. That man Mr Mbethe played his cards well.

V/O: Dineo Lewis worked as an admin officer for the Kuruman Community Trust.

Dineo: I was so discouraged because really what was promised was not happening.

V/O: Godisang Itumeleng is one of the village leaders.
00:01:53
Godisang: They promised us that when the mine starts operating, we will get shares.

Masa: When you ask them about the money from the mine and the trust, what do they say?

Godisang: They say we don’t have shares in the trust, and even that trust is owned by Mr Mbethe and his children, and that’s it.

V/O: Instead of gold and silver, the beneficiaries get a food parcel in December.

Nnuku: The groceries, they are not even edible because some of them they have expired. Some of them are very small.

V/O: Nnuku Matilo is a community activist who the beneficiaries approached for help.

Nnuku: You can imagine waiting for the whole year for 5kg.

V/O: KCT told Carte Blanche they distribute over 54 000 food parcels every year, but beneficiaries say these are mostly from the mine NOT the trust.

Link: This is what the trust gave to the beneficiaries in the Christmas hamper last year. Some flour, tinned fish, jam, coffee creamer, rice and brown sugar, a packet of tea and maize meal, all for a grand total of about R1200. I mean, it's like they’re saying, oh, let them eat pap.

V/O: Not that Mbethe and his colleagues weren’t generous with their advice: “Why not start companies to service the mine? Like a laundry business, for example.”

V/O: So each village had to open a company under a cooperative, called Kuruman Community Mining and Other Projects. KCMO has contracts with the mine.

V/O: So, in a very useful arrangement for some, the mine continued paying dividends into the TRUST, while the beneficiaries get a mere thousand rand a YEAR – from KCMO – their own company! Rather than sharing in the windfall, the beneficiaries are, in effect, paying themselves!

Nnuku: Are you saying that when I’m getting a thousand rand a year I’m benefiting? That’s not a benefit. It’s a shame. And on that thousand-rand years go by, things change. There’s inflation, there’s whatever. But that thousand rand does not change.

VO: But the shame doesn’t end there… coming up, we continue our investigation and find promises of prosperity broken by the politically connected, and a community that's had enough.


End of PART 1.

PART 2:

VO: We’re in the Northern Cape manganese fields where the new black gold is making a mine called UMK and its shareholders fabulously wealthy: a Russian conglomerate and the ANC's Chancellor House. But a community trust meant to benefit over 500 of the poorest of the poor is big on promises, short on delivery – and the beneficiaries want answers.

UPS: Cell phone footage

VO: Among the mine’s Russian investors is a company run by this man, Viktor Vekselberg, a multi-billionaire squeezed by international sanctions but warmly welcomed on our shores.

Stefaans: He met amongst others the Mining Minster Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka at the time, and Thabo Mbeki, the President at the time.

VO: The Kuruman Community Trust is an indirect shareholder in the mine, but beneficiaries say they only get a thousand rand a year and a food parcel. And, the money doesn’t even come from the TRUST, but from a cooperative owned by the beneficiaries themselves!

Link: So, what can you do with a thousand rand a year? That’s R83 a month. R83! That’s about a loaf of bread per week.

V/O: And to get that pittance they have to spend money. Molly Mabe lives in Gadiboye with her disabled son.
00:09:50
Molly: I have to get a paper from the bank for me to be able to get that money.

Masa: Where do you take it?

Molly: And then I take it to the office of Pitsa ya Setshaba.

V/O: It’s an hour to Kuruman by taxi.

Molly: Yes, R80 - R40 there and R40 back.
00:11:56
Masa: So, when you come back it’s no longer R1000, it’s now less than that?

Molly: Yes.

Masa: Now you’ve only got R920 to work with.

Dineo: When the mine started working, all of a sudden there were changes.

V/O: As an admin officer for the trust, Dineo Lewis had an inside view. She says most agreements were verbal and the trust’s founder, Lazarus Mbethe, claimed he never promised anyone shares.

Masa: And so, he just went against his word?

Dineo: And we started to hear that the Trust belongs to him.

V/O: Lazarus Mbethe is also a Director of UMK, as well as Majestic Silver Trading 40 and Pitsa ya Setshaba, both shareholders in the mine.

Masa: In the 10 years and 4 months that you worked for the Trust, did you ever get to see the financials?

Dineo: No.

Emily: Hoe gaan dit meneer, dumelang!

V/O: In fact, we didn’t find a single beneficiary who’d seen the trust’s books.

So just how much money has it received from the mine?

Based on the financial statements of Renova Manganese Investments in the last 10 years, UMK declared and paid dividends of over $486 million to its shareholders.

As a shareholder of Majestic Silver Trading, the beneficiaries of the Kuruman Community Trust should have received almost $20 million – well over R300 million. So where has that money gone?

Masa: The Trust has been operating for years now, what difference has it made in your lives?

Monica: We don’t see one. There’s absolutely no difference, they’re not doing anything.

V/O: Monica Letlhoanye is a beneficiary demanding her share.

Monica: Life is hard! Life is hard, plus there’s no work. We’re unemployed, our children are unemployed, there’s nothing. We survive on social grants.

V/O: But while the beneficiaries dwell in deprivation, the Russian shareholders face First World problems. In 2018 the Renova Group and Viktor Vekselberg were sanctioned by the United Sates. Renova responded by changing its name to New African Manganese Investments registered in Cyprus. Vekselberg responded by putting his house in a plush American suburb on the market.

V/O: But after Russia invaded Ukraine last year, the noose tightened around Vekselberg and his oligarchs.

Garland: Today, at the request of the United States Department of Justice, Spanish authorities seized a super yacht belonging to a sanctioned Russian oligarch.

V/O: Not only did Vekselberg lose his yacht, but also his jet, his house he’d tried to sell, and his luxury apartment in Manhattan valued at $11 million. His bank accounts holding $1.5 billion were also frozen.

Nnuku: They are living large. You can imagine the Russian who is sitting in Russia with the yachts and all those luxury, whereas the people that went to toyi-toyi, to say we want this mining right, they are living in shame.

V/O: So what is it about Russia and its controversial business moguls that appears so enticing to the ANC? Is it the party’s historical ties to Moscow especially during the liberation struggle? Something no better demonstrated than our government’s refusal to condemn Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Ray: And it's true, Russia did support the ANC in exile, did support the struggle against apartheid. But it’s more nuanced than that. I mean the first groupings of ANC exiles that went for training in Russia were trained in Ukraine at Odessa and other places in Ukraine. So that, you know, it's a bit simplistic to sort of now historically associate Russia and not Ukraine with that history.

V/O: Whatever the reason, it’s a relationship that’s bearing fruit… for some. In the minutes of a 2007 meeting of the KCT, struggle veteran and Trustee, Major General Jackie Sedibe, couldn’t have been clearer about who exactly was benefitting…
Text: “…it is for the first time the ANC as a party is given the opportunity to own a mining business.” – Major General Jackie Sedibe

VO: Not an individual or a company. The party.

Link: Some of the Trust’s beneficiaries were too scared to talk to us on camera because they said “This is an ANC mine.” That perception is well-founded – and while the 540 beneficiaries may not be benefiting much from the mine, the ruling party certainly is.

Stefaans: Between UMK, Majestic Silver and Chancellor House, at least R55 million went to the ANC over these two years. You don’t bite the hand that feeds you. Well, there’s a lot of feeding that’s happening there.

V/O: Even last year’s ANC elective conference was part funded by UMK to the tune of R15 million.

Link: We requested an interview from Lazarus Mbethe to find out how much money is in the Trust and where it's going? His PR company wrote back to say that Mr Mbethe would not be available to participate in an interview.

V/O: Instead they told us about their flagship project, the state-of-the art mobile medical centre that services the Kuruman community. But “mobile” is an overstatement: Here it is on the grounds of an existing clinic in GaMopedi.

Nnuku: How do we expect a mobile clinic to go and stand in Tshwaragang community hospital, when the 27 villages don’t have clinics? So if this clinic was indeed for the community, it would be on the outskirts, in the rurals, serving the real beneficiaries of the Trust.

V/O: Before leaving Kuruman, we visited another of KCT’s much-vaunted projects: the sinking of a borehole in each of the 27 villages.

Masa: Did they say the borehole is for the whole village?

Lettie: Yes.

V/O: But the boreholes are being sunk in the yards of the village leaders, like Letty Dibakwe in Manyeding

Lettie: They are going to pull electricity, and as I am using electricity all the people who need water will contribute to the electricity.

V/O: The borehole “project” was announced by trustee, George Fanampe. We called him to ask a few questions about the Trust.

Fanampe: Dumela.

Masa: Mr Fanampe. you are speaking to Masa Kekana from Carte Blanche. Mr Fanampe we would like to arrange an interview with you, we can come to your offices, perhaps tomorrow?

Fanampe: You are calling me from Carte Blanche?

Masa: Yes. The television program.

Fanampe: Where did you get this number from?

Masa: We got the number from our sources. We'd like to talk to you about the Kuruman Community Trust.

Fanampe: My advice being to go to your sources.

V/O: Tired of being stonewalled, the beneficiaries have now lawyered up and are represented by Louise du Plessis from Lawyers for Human Rights.

Masa: Should these beneficiaries have had access to those financials?

Louise: Of course they must have, they are the beneficiaries. They will have to give us the financial statements, Trust deed, any other documents, shareholder agreements, any other agreements that the Trust entered into on behalf of the beneficiaries.

V/O: UMK declined an interview, saying they have no legal authority over the affairs of the Kuruman Community Trust. Repeated requests for comment from Chancellor House, Majestic Silver Trading, the ANC and the DMR were ignored.

VO: We were, it seems, getting a taste of what the beneficiaries have been through for close to two decades.

Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 24 July 2023 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: LET THEM EAT PAP – FINAL V/O: Imagine being told you’ve been chosen as a beneficiary of a manganese mine. You and 20 other people in your village are now part of a Trust. Your lives will change, you will be lifted out of poverty, and when the mine opens, you’ll be employed. You even get bused all the way to Pretoria to meet the Deputy Minister of Mineral Resources. Doreen: She said I don’t want to hear any child from Kuruman saying they are struggling to get a job, because we are issuing a mining license. Pause for sound of explosion V/O: Eighteen years later the mine is flourishing, but you are still unemployed and struggling to survive. FADE TO BLACK Tidimalo: You can see the house we live in. They’re not houses that should be housing seven people. This house is too small for seven people. V/O: Poverty has settled on the Moncho family like a second skin. We met Tidimalo going to fetch water, but the only tap in the village was dry. It makes it harder to care for her sick father who is frail and confined to bed. Sfx: Tidimalo talking to her Dad Tidimalo: We survive on my dad’s social grant, and the kids’ social grant – only. No one in our family works. That means when my dad dies…it’s a story. V/O: The Northern Cape has rampant unemployment, few opportunities, and a growing alcohol and drug problem. But beneath this red soil lies 80% of the world’s manganese. It’s a booming industry – so why is this community still poor? When mining rights were nationalized in 2004, it presented huge opportunities for black empowerment. Stefaans Brümmer was a journalist for the Mail & Guardian at the time. Stefaans: The Department of Minerals said it’s going to give these rights only to BEE companies, and then a technical and financial partner would be brought in after the award of the mining rights. V/O: Enter billionaire Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg, owner of the Renova Group – a conglomerate with interests in telecoms, energy and – yes - mining. Stefaans: So Vekselberg is a typical Russian oligarch. V/O: The oligarchs are politically influential businessmen who made their fortunes when state-run industries were privatised, after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Stefaans: So, Vekselberg made his money out of oil fields and especially bauxite mining. V/O: In 2004 Vekselberg was worth $10 billion. He splashed out on nine priceless Fabergé eggs which are housed in his private museum in St Petersburg. He also visited South Africa for the first time - on the lookout for mining investment opportunities. Stefaans: He met amongst others the Mining Minster Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka at the time, and Thabo Mbeki, the President at the time. Masa: So, he had access to some powerful people? Stefaans: Clearly, he had some diplomatic backing also from the Russian side, and I think he was able to make a grand entrance. Text: “Renova masters Africa” headline V/O: Vekselberg’s attention was directed to the Northern Cape manganese fields by an investment arm of the ANC - Chancellor House - named after the building in downtown Joburg that originally housed the law firm of Mandela and Tambo. 00:08:24 Stefaans: Chancellor House was set up around 2003. It was set up simply to fund the ANC. And I think there were a number of meetings between Renova and ANC officials. V/O: He also met Lazarus Mbethe, a politically connected businessman from Mpumalanga involved in coal mining, security and farming. Mbethe’s company Pitsa ya Setshaba – meaning community pot - applied for the mining rights, but these could only be awarded if the local Kuruman community was included in the venture. Nelson: People of Kuruman were exploited. V/O: Nelson Hantise is the Chairperson of the John Taole Gaetsewe Civic Organisation. Nelson: Mbethe pushed to open the mine, to say you are the local people, you are the beneficiary, or you are the shareholder. Come, come, come, come, I’m opening the mine, help me to get the licence. V/O: The Kuruman Community Trust was founded by Mbethe in 2005. He selected 20 people from 27 villages around the Kuruman area - a total of 540 beneficiaries. He bused representatives from each village to the DMR in Pretoria. Motlalepula: When we went there, they said we are going to sign for the opening of the mine. V/O: Motlalepula Mosetlo was one of the beneficiaries on the bus. Motlalepula: And when the mine opened, they will take us first – we who are suffering and uneducated - to work at the mine. V/O: With promises of employment, education, roads and clinics, Doreen Ntsheyagae felt they were on the road to the promised land. Masa: When you left there, were you happy? Doreen: Yes, we were very happy, like the children of Canaan coming from Egypt, promised gold and silver. But we didn’t know what was going to happen. We only knew that there is a mine, and when they talk about a mine it means work. V/O: And so it came to pass, that United Manganese of Kalahari opened in 2005, with Lazarus Mbethe as Chairman of a joint venture between Renova and BEE partner Majestic Silver Trading 40 – a consortium with strong political links. Majestic Silver Trading is made up of Chancellor House and Pitsa ya Setshaba, with Kuruman Community Trust getting 8% of the shares. Stefaans: Vekselberg’s relationship with the ANC, getting into bed with Chancellor House for example, I don’t think it is necessarily because he believes in what the ANC stands for. It was simply sucking up to power. That’s what oligarchs do. V/O: The Brenthurst Foundation’s Ray Hartley agrees. Ray: There are people within the ANC who admire the Russian oligarchic system where you have a political elite and a bunch of elite businesses around that are making a lot of money out of that elite, and contracts being shared amongst friends and all that kind of thing, which is the way Russia works. V/O: In 2006 Russian President Vladimir Putin came to South Africa on a State Visit, accompanied by a large business delegation. Leading that delegation was none other than Viktor Vekselberg with promises of investment in infrastructure. And money talks. The licence was granted and UMK started mining in 2008. Five years later they celebrated their joint venture. Mbethe: I believe our mine it’s a real Northern Cape success story. Indeed, a South African success story. Konstantin: UMK mine is the most positive example of cooperation between Russia and South Africa. V/O: Cooperation witnessed by Presidents Putin and Zuma when Viktor Vekselberg and Lazarus Mbethe signed agreements in Durban. Link: This is the mine that has rained riches on its Russian and South African shareholders – as much as R2.4 billion a year. But while they’ve been divvying up the dosh, it seems the local community that was used to unlock that wealth has been left out in the cold. Dineo: The people were used. That man Mr Mbethe played his cards well. V/O: Dineo Lewis worked as an admin officer for the Kuruman Community Trust. Dineo: I was so discouraged because really what was promised was not happening. V/O: Godisang Itumeleng is one of the village leaders. 00:01:53 Godisang: They promised us that when the mine starts operating, we will get shares. Masa: When you ask them about the money from the mine and the trust, what do they say? Godisang: They say we don’t have shares in the trust, and even that trust is owned by Mr Mbethe and his children, and that’s it. V/O: Instead of gold and silver, the beneficiaries get a food parcel in December. Nnuku: The groceries, they are not even edible because some of them they have expired. Some of them are very small. V/O: Nnuku Matilo is a community activist who the beneficiaries approached for help. Nnuku: You can imagine waiting for the whole year for 5kg. V/O: KCT told Carte Blanche they distribute over 54 000 food parcels every year, but beneficiaries say these are mostly from the mine NOT the trust. Link: This is what the trust gave to the beneficiaries in the Christmas hamper last year. Some flour, tinned fish, jam, coffee creamer, rice and brown sugar, a packet of tea and maize meal, all for a grand total of about R1200. I mean, it's like they’re saying, oh, let them eat pap. V/O: Not that Mbethe and his colleagues weren’t generous with their advice: “Why not start companies to service the mine? Like a laundry business, for example.” V/O: So each village had to open a company under a cooperative, called Kuruman Community Mining and Other Projects. KCMO has contracts with the mine. V/O: So, in a very useful arrangement for some, the mine continued paying dividends into the TRUST, while the beneficiaries get a mere thousand rand a YEAR – from KCMO – their own company! Rather than sharing in the windfall, the beneficiaries are, in effect, paying themselves! Nnuku: Are you saying that when I’m getting a thousand rand a year I’m benefiting? That’s not a benefit. It’s a shame. And on that thousand-rand years go by, things change. There’s inflation, there’s whatever. But that thousand rand does not change. VO: But the shame doesn’t end there… coming up, we continue our investigation and find promises of prosperity broken by the politically connected, and a community that's had enough. End of PART 1. PART 2: VO: We’re in the Northern Cape manganese fields where the new black gold is making a mine called UMK and its shareholders fabulously wealthy: a Russian conglomerate and the ANC's Chancellor House. But a community trust meant to benefit over 500 of the poorest of the poor is big on promises, short on delivery – and the beneficiaries want answers. UPS: Cell phone footage VO: Among the mine’s Russian investors is a company run by this man, Viktor Vekselberg, a multi-billionaire squeezed by international sanctions but warmly welcomed on our shores. Stefaans: He met amongst others the Mining Minster Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka at the time, and Thabo Mbeki, the President at the time. VO: The Kuruman Community Trust is an indirect shareholder in the mine, but beneficiaries say they only get a thousand rand a year and a food parcel. And, the money doesn’t even come from the TRUST, but from a cooperative owned by the beneficiaries themselves! Link: So, what can you do with a thousand rand a year? That’s R83 a month. R83! That’s about a loaf of bread per week. V/O: And to get that pittance they have to spend money. Molly Mabe lives in Gadiboye with her disabled son. 00:09:50 Molly: I have to get a paper from the bank for me to be able to get that money. Masa: Where do you take it? Molly: And then I take it to the office of Pitsa ya Setshaba. V/O: It’s an hour to Kuruman by taxi. Molly: Yes, R80 - R40 there and R40 back. 00:11:56 Masa: So, when you come back it’s no longer R1000, it’s now less than that? Molly: Yes. Masa: Now you’ve only got R920 to work with. Dineo: When the mine started working, all of a sudden there were changes. V/O: As an admin officer for the trust, Dineo Lewis had an inside view. She says most agreements were verbal and the trust’s founder, Lazarus Mbethe, claimed he never promised anyone shares. Masa: And so, he just went against his word? Dineo: And we started to hear that the Trust belongs to him. V/O: Lazarus Mbethe is also a Director of UMK, as well as Majestic Silver Trading 40 and Pitsa ya Setshaba, both shareholders in the mine. Masa: In the 10 years and 4 months that you worked for the Trust, did you ever get to see the financials? Dineo: No. Emily: Hoe gaan dit meneer, dumelang! V/O: In fact, we didn’t find a single beneficiary who’d seen the trust’s books. So just how much money has it received from the mine? Based on the financial statements of Renova Manganese Investments in the last 10 years, UMK declared and paid dividends of over $486 million to its shareholders. As a shareholder of Majestic Silver Trading, the beneficiaries of the Kuruman Community Trust should have received almost $20 million – well over R300 million. So where has that money gone? Masa: The Trust has been operating for years now, what difference has it made in your lives? Monica: We don’t see one. There’s absolutely no difference, they’re not doing anything. V/O: Monica Letlhoanye is a beneficiary demanding her share. Monica: Life is hard! Life is hard, plus there’s no work. We’re unemployed, our children are unemployed, there’s nothing. We survive on social grants. V/O: But while the beneficiaries dwell in deprivation, the Russian shareholders face First World problems. In 2018 the Renova Group and Viktor Vekselberg were sanctioned by the United Sates. Renova responded by changing its name to New African Manganese Investments registered in Cyprus. Vekselberg responded by putting his house in a plush American suburb on the market. V/O: But after Russia invaded Ukraine last year, the noose tightened around Vekselberg and his oligarchs. Garland: Today, at the request of the United States Department of Justice, Spanish authorities seized a super yacht belonging to a sanctioned Russian oligarch. V/O: Not only did Vekselberg lose his yacht, but also his jet, his house he’d tried to sell, and his luxury apartment in Manhattan valued at $11 million. His bank accounts holding $1.5 billion were also frozen. Nnuku: They are living large. You can imagine the Russian who is sitting in Russia with the yachts and all those luxury, whereas the people that went to toyi-toyi, to say we want this mining right, they are living in shame. V/O: So what is it about Russia and its controversial business moguls that appears so enticing to the ANC? Is it the party’s historical ties to Moscow especially during the liberation struggle? Something no better demonstrated than our government’s refusal to condemn Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ray: And it's true, Russia did support the ANC in exile, did support the struggle against apartheid. But it’s more nuanced than that. I mean the first groupings of ANC exiles that went for training in Russia were trained in Ukraine at Odessa and other places in Ukraine. So that, you know, it's a bit simplistic to sort of now historically associate Russia and not Ukraine with that history. V/O: Whatever the reason, it’s a relationship that’s bearing fruit… for some. In the minutes of a 2007 meeting of the KCT, struggle veteran and Trustee, Major General Jackie Sedibe, couldn’t have been clearer about who exactly was benefitting… Text: “…it is for the first time the ANC as a party is given the opportunity to own a mining business.” – Major General Jackie Sedibe VO: Not an individual or a company. The party. Link: Some of the Trust’s beneficiaries were too scared to talk to us on camera because they said “This is an ANC mine.” That perception is well-founded – and while the 540 beneficiaries may not be benefiting much from the mine, the ruling party certainly is. Stefaans: Between UMK, Majestic Silver and Chancellor House, at least R55 million went to the ANC over these two years. You don’t bite the hand that feeds you. Well, there’s a lot of feeding that’s happening there. V/O: Even last year’s ANC elective conference was part funded by UMK to the tune of R15 million. Link: We requested an interview from Lazarus Mbethe to find out how much money is in the Trust and where it's going? His PR company wrote back to say that Mr Mbethe would not be available to participate in an interview. V/O: Instead they told us about their flagship project, the state-of-the art mobile medical centre that services the Kuruman community. But “mobile” is an overstatement: Here it is on the grounds of an existing clinic in GaMopedi. Nnuku: How do we expect a mobile clinic to go and stand in Tshwaragang community hospital, when the 27 villages don’t have clinics? So if this clinic was indeed for the community, it would be on the outskirts, in the rurals, serving the real beneficiaries of the Trust. V/O: Before leaving Kuruman, we visited another of KCT’s much-vaunted projects: the sinking of a borehole in each of the 27 villages. Masa: Did they say the borehole is for the whole village? Lettie: Yes. V/O: But the boreholes are being sunk in the yards of the village leaders, like Letty Dibakwe in Manyeding Lettie: They are going to pull electricity, and as I am using electricity all the people who need water will contribute to the electricity. V/O: The borehole “project” was announced by trustee, George Fanampe. We called him to ask a few questions about the Trust. Fanampe: Dumela. Masa: Mr Fanampe. you are speaking to Masa Kekana from Carte Blanche. Mr Fanampe we would like to arrange an interview with you, we can come to your offices, perhaps tomorrow? Fanampe: You are calling me from Carte Blanche? Masa: Yes. The television program. Fanampe: Where did you get this number from? Masa: We got the number from our sources. We'd like to talk to you about the Kuruman Community Trust. Fanampe: My advice being to go to your sources. V/O: Tired of being stonewalled, the beneficiaries have now lawyered up and are represented by Louise du Plessis from Lawyers for Human Rights. Masa: Should these beneficiaries have had access to those financials? Louise: Of course they must have, they are the beneficiaries. They will have to give us the financial statements, Trust deed, any other documents, shareholder agreements, any other agreements that the Trust entered into on behalf of the beneficiaries. V/O: UMK declined an interview, saying they have no legal authority over the affairs of the Kuruman Community Trust. Repeated requests for comment from Chancellor House, Majestic Silver Trading, the ANC and the DMR were ignored. VO: We were, it seems, getting a taste of what the beneficiaries have been through for close to two decades.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): They're shareholders in the 4th largest manganese mine in South Africa, but instead of annual dividends, all they get is R1000 a year and a Christmas food hamper.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Interviews with some of the 540 community members who were promised education bursaries, job opportunities, health care and upliftment of their 27 villages when they became shareholders in Pitsa ya Setshaba (The Community Pot) the entity that was awarded the prospecting rights for the United Manganese of Kalahari mine near Hotazel. According to legislation, this mining community Trust (KCT) was established as a pre-requisite to prospecting and mining rights. Two busloads of villagers (+- 150 people) were taken to Pretoria to meet Dept of Mineral Resources Minister Susan Shabangu in 2005, as evidence of community involvement and benefit. Instead of enrichment they are still living in abject poverty and only a select few are benefiting from the hugely profitable mine.
metadata.Summary: In 2004 Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg arrived in South Africa looking for manganese mining opportunities and a BEE partner who could win the mining rights. Several ANC-connected entities jostled for the privilege. Lazarus Mbethe representing Pitsa ya Setshaba won the privilege, but his consortium had to include the ANC's Chancellor House and the Kuruman Community Trust. Together they owned 51% of UMK in a company called Majestic Silver Trading. Viktor Vekselberg's Renova owned 49% and invested $350m to build the mine. In a 2006 State visit to South Africa President Vladimir Putin consolidated this partnership, with Vekselberg promising to invest a further $2billion for a manganese smelter at Coega. UMK is now a fabulously profitable mine (R2.4 billion a year) but the community are receiving very little benefit. Individuals receive R1000 a year, and a Christmas food hamper. Lazarus Mbethe is the sole Trustee of the Kuruman Community Trust, but the community never see any financial statements. They believe they were simply used to get the mining rights to make ANC comrades rich, while they continue to live lives of hardship - in villages with no running water, no electricity, no inside toilets, no jobs, and surviving only on pensions and government grants. The KCT boasts only three community projects: the goat project - now defunct; the brick making project - taken over by a private individual, and the mobile clinic project - still operational but only in villages that already have a clinic. Most of the people I met with didn't know of its existence and only one person had never seen it. It is parked in the grounds of the
metadata.Further information: The ANC benefit hugely from the UMK mine, being the recipients of annual donations by UMK, Chancellor House, and Majestic Silver Trading. It is clear from meeting minutes as far back as 2007 that the ANC regards this mine as and ANC mine, and villagers are scared to speak up saying "they can kill us". The ANC's reluctance to condemn Russia's invasion of Ukraine is partly explained by their partnership with Renova in this mine. They are dependent on the Russians for their income.
